sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Computers store data with mechanical disks, solid-state flash, removable media, and optical media. Multiple drives can also be combined in RAID configurations for performance, fault tolerance, or both.
Objective 3.4 tests whether you can distinguish the storage technology, communication interface, physical form factor, drive configuration, and intended purpose.
sections.callout: TECHNOLOGY → INTERFACE → FORM FACTOR → CONFIGURATION → PURPOSE

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes storage speed, physical size, connection method, fault tolerance, or portability, identify which storage characteristic the clue is testing.

sections.title: Hard Drives
paragraphs: A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on rotating platters. Its mechanical components include platters, a spindle, and read/write heads.
sections.callout: Mechanical drive with spinning magnetic platters → HDD.

sections.title: Spindle Speeds
paragraphs: Spindle speed describes how quickly an HDD's platters rotate and is measured in revolutions per minute (RPM). Common examples include 5,400, 7,200, and 10,000 RPM.
bullets: Higher RPM can improve access performance, although RPM is not the only performance factor.
SSDs have no spindle speed because they contain no rotating platters.
sections.callout: An RPM value identifies a mechanical hard drive characteristic.

sections.title: Hard-Drive Form Factors
paragraphs: Hard-drive form factors describe physical size. Objective 3.4 requires you to compare 2.5-inch and 3.5-inch drives.
sections.callout: Form factor describes physical dimensions, not capacity or speed.

sections.title: 2.5-Inch Drive
paragraphs: The 2.5-inch form factor is smaller and is commonly associated with laptops, compact computers, and some external drives.
sections.callout: Laptop mechanical drive → 2.5-inch HDD.

sections.title: 3.5-Inch Drive
paragraphs: The 3.5-inch form factor is larger and is commonly associated with desktop computers, workstations, servers, and large-capacity storage systems.
sections.callout: Standard desktop mechanical drive → 3.5-inch HDD.

sections.title: 2.5-Inch vs. 3.5-Inch
sections.callout: Laptop → 2.5-inch. Desktop HDD → 3.5-inch.

sections.title: Solid-State Drives
paragraphs: A Solid-State Drive (SSD) stores data in non-volatile flash memory. It has no spinning platter or moving read/write head.
sections.callout: Storage with no moving parts → SSD.

sections.title: HDD vs. SSD
sections.callout: HDD = SPIN. SSD = FLASH.

sections.title: SSD Communication Interfaces
paragraphs: Storage terminology can describe different layers. For Objective 3.4, distinguish Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe), Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SATA), Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe), and Serial Attached SCSI (SAS).
sections.callout: Ask how the storage device communicates with the system.

sections.title: SATA Storage Interface
paragraphs: Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SATA) is a common storage interface used by hard drives, SATA SSDs, and optical drives. A SATA SSD is still solid-state storage; SATA identifies how it communicates.
sections.callout: 2.5-inch SSD using the traditional SATA interface → SATA SSD.

sections.title: PCIe Storage Interface
paragraphs: Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) is a high-speed system interface used by many devices, including high-performance storage. PCIe offers substantially more bandwidth than traditional SATA.
sections.callout: High-speed storage pathway → PCIe.

sections.title: Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe)
paragraphs: Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) is a storage communication protocol designed for fast non-volatile storage over PCIe. It avoids limitations inherited from protocols designed for older disk technologies.
sections.callout: High-speed PCIe storage protocol → NVMe.

sections.title: NVMe vs. PCIe

table.caption: Protocol and pathway
rows: Storage language traveling on the road

sections.callout: Protocol clue → NVMe. Underlying bus clue → PCIe.

sections.title: SATA vs. NVMe
paragraphs: Both SATA and NVMe can be used with SSDs. SATA follows a traditional storage-interface architecture, while NVMe is optimized for high-performance flash storage over PCIe.
sections.callout: SSD does not automatically mean NVMe.

sections.title: Serial Attached SCSI (SAS)
paragraphs: Serial Attached SCSI (SAS) is a storage interface commonly used in servers, enterprise storage, and storage arrays where reliability and high performance are important.
sections.callout: Enterprise or server storage interface → SAS.

sections.title: SATA vs. SAS

table.caption: Common storage-interface scenarios
rows: Requires a compatible controller and platform

sections.callout: SATA = everyday storage. SAS = enterprise storage.

sections.title: SSD Form Factors
paragraphs: SSD form factors describe physical design. Objective 3.4 requires you to distinguish M.2 from Mini-Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (mSATA). A form factor does not always identify the protocol.
sections.callout: Form factor tells you physical design.

sections.title: M.2
paragraphs: M.2 is a compact card-style form factor commonly used for SSDs that install directly into compatible motherboard slots. Depending on both drive and slot, an M.2 SSD may use SATA or PCIe/NVMe.
sections.callout: Small motherboard-mounted SSD module → M.2.

sections.title: M.2 Form Factor vs. NVMe
sections.callout: M.2 = SHAPE. NVMe = COMMUNICATION.

sections.title: Mini-Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (mSATA)
paragraphs: mSATA is a compact SSD form factor and interface based on SATA technology. It appeared in smaller systems before M.2 became more common.
sections.callout: Compact older SATA-based SSD → mSATA.

sections.title: M.2 vs. mSATA
paragraphs: M.2 and mSATA can look similar, but they are different standards. M.2 is a newer flexible module format that can support different interfaces, while mSATA is an older SATA-based design.
sections.callout: Similar appearance does not make M.2 and mSATA interchangeable.

sections.title: Drive Configurations
paragraphs: Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) combines multiple drives for increased performance, fault tolerance, or both. Objective 3.4 requires RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10.
sections.callout: RAID recognition words: STRIPE, MIRROR, PARITY.

sections.title: RAID 0
paragraphs: RAID 0 uses striping to spread data across at least two drives. It can improve performance but provides no fault tolerance; failure of one drive destroys the array's data.
sections.callout: RAID 0 = striping and ZERO redundancy.

sections.title: RAID 1
paragraphs: RAID 1 uses mirroring. In a basic two-drive mirror, the same data is written to both drives, and either drive can preserve the data if the other fails. Usable capacity is approximately one drive's capacity.
sections.callout: RAID 1 = one copy mirrors another.

sections.title: RAID 0 vs. RAID 1

table.caption: Striping and mirroring
rows: One drive in a basic two-drive mirror

sections.callout: 0 = speed with zero protection. 1 = mirror.

sections.title: RAID 5
paragraphs: RAID 5 uses striping with distributed single parity. It requires at least three drives and can tolerate one drive failure.
bullets: Approximate usable capacity: (number of drives - 1) × smallest drive capacity
Three 2 TB drives provide about 4 TB usable
sections.callout: RAID 5 = stripe + single parity + one-drive fault tolerance.

sections.title: RAID 6
paragraphs: RAID 6 uses striping with dual distributed parity. It requires at least four drives and can tolerate two drive failures.
bullets: Approximate usable capacity: (number of drives - 2) × smallest drive capacity
Four 2 TB drives provide about 4 TB usable
sections.callout: RAID 6 = stripe + dual parity + two-drive fault tolerance.

sections.title: RAID 5 vs. RAID 6
sections.callout: RAID 5 → one may fail. RAID 6 → two may fail.

sections.title: RAID 10
paragraphs: RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping across at least four drives. It provides strong performance and fault tolerance without parity.
sections.callout: RAID 10 = MIRROR + STRIPE.

sections.title: RAID 10 Fault Tolerance
paragraphs: RAID 10 can survive drive failures while each mirrored set retains a working member. It may survive more than one failure, but only when both members of the same mirror are not lost.
sections.callout: Which drives fail matters; do not claim RAID 10 always survives any two failures.

sections.title: RAID Comparison

table.caption: Required RAID levels
rows: One drive in a basic mirror

sections.callout: 0 STRIPE | 1 MIRROR | 5 ONE PARITY | 6 TWO PARITY | 10 MIRROR + STRIPE

sections.title: RAID Is Not a Backup
paragraphs: RAID can improve performance, redundancy, or availability, but it does not replace a separate recoverable backup. It does not inherently protect against accidental deletion, malware, file corruption, theft, fire, or destruction of the entire system.
sections.callout: RAID keeps storage available. Backup preserves a separate recoverable copy.

sections.title: Removable Storage
paragraphs: Removable storage is designed to be connected, removed, and transported easily. Objective 3.4 includes flash drives and memory cards.
sections.callout: Portable flash media → flash drive or memory card.

sections.title: Flash Drives
paragraphs: A USB flash drive places non-volatile flash memory in a portable device with a USB connection. Common uses include moving files, portable storage, installation media, and recovery tools.
sections.callout: Small USB device used to transport files → flash drive.

sections.title: Memory Cards
paragraphs: A memory card is compact removable flash storage commonly used in cameras, smartphones, tablets, embedded devices, and other portable electronics.
sections.callout: Camera-style removable flash media → memory card.

sections.title: Flash Drive vs. Memory Card

table.caption: Two forms of removable flash storage
rows: Usually has its own USB connector
Inserts into a card slot or reader

sections.callout: USB stick → flash drive. Card slot → memory card.

sections.title: Optical Drives
paragraphs: An optical drive reads and sometimes writes laser-based media such as CD, DVD, and Blu-ray. Uses include software installation, media playback, data distribution, and removable archival media.
sections.callout: Laser-readable disc → optical drive.

sections.title: Optical vs. Magnetic vs. Flash Storage

table.caption: Storage mechanism comparison
rows: Memory chips and no moving parts

sections.callout: SPINNING MAGNET → HDD. CHIPS → FLASH. LASER DISC → OPTICAL.

sections.title: Objective 3.4 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Storage questions can mix technology, interface, protocol, form factor, and RAID configuration. Identify which layer each clue describes before answering.

entries.title: HDD vs. SSD
paragraphs: RPM and spinning platters indicate HDD. Flash and no moving parts indicate SSD.

entries.title: 2.5-Inch vs. 3.5-Inch
paragraphs: These describe physical drive size, not interface, capacity, or speed.

entries.title: SATA vs. NVMe
paragraphs: SATA is a traditional storage interface family. NVMe is a high-performance storage protocol commonly using PCIe.
entries.memoryHook: An SSD is not automatically NVMe

entries.title: M.2 vs. NVMe
paragraphs: M.2 is a form factor; NVMe is a protocol. An M.2 drive can use SATA or NVMe.

entries.title: PCIe vs. NVMe
paragraphs: PCIe is the bus/interface; NVMe is the storage protocol.

entries.title: SATA vs. SAS
paragraphs: SATA is common in consumer storage; SAS is common in enterprise and server storage.

entries.title: M.2 vs. mSATA
paragraphs: M.2 is a newer flexible module standard; mSATA is an older SATA-based compact design.
entries.memoryHook: Small cards can still be different standards

entries.title: RAID 0 vs. RAID 1
paragraphs: RAID 0 stripes for performance without fault tolerance. RAID 1 mirrors for redundancy.

entries.title: RAID 5 vs. RAID 6
paragraphs: RAID 5 uses single parity and tolerates one drive failure. RAID 6 uses dual parity and tolerates two.

entries.title: RAID 1 vs. RAID 10
paragraphs: RAID 1 mirrors; RAID 10 combines mirrored sets with striping for performance and redundancy.

entries.title: RAID 0 vs. RAID 10
paragraphs: Both stripe, but RAID 10 stripes across mirrored sets while RAID 0 has no redundancy.

entries.title: RAID vs. Backup
paragraphs: RAID redundancy is not a separate recoverable backup copy.

entries.title: Flash Drive vs. Memory Card
paragraphs: A flash drive usually has its own USB connector; a memory card uses a compatible reader or slot.

sections.title: Storage Scenario Workflow
bullets: Identify the storage mechanism: magnetic, flash, or optical.
Identify the communication interface or protocol: SATA, PCIe, NVMe, or SAS.
Identify the physical form factor: 2.5-inch, 3.5-inch, M.2, or mSATA.
Identify the configuration: single drive or required RAID level.
Identify the purpose: performance, fault tolerance, portability, or optical-media access.
sections.callout: TECHNOLOGY → INTERFACE → FORM FACTOR → CONFIGURATION → PURPOSE

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Small motherboard SSD form factor → M.2
Removable camera-style flash storage → memory card
CD, DVD, or Blu-ray → optical drive
sections.callout: HDD → SPIN | SSD → FLASH | M.2 → FORM FACTOR | NVMe → PROTOCOL | PCIe → PATHWAY
